info.title: What are Btrfs subvolumes and snapshots?

abstract.para: Btrfs subvolumes and snapshots are the basis of &snapper;. This chapter explains both concepts and describes how snapshots use disk space.

section.title: Btrfs Subvolumes
section.para: Btrfs subvolumes are separately mountable file systems within a physical partition. A Btrfs file system is set up with subvolumes by default. Each subvolume has its own independent file and directory hierarchy. Unlike Logical Volume Manager (LVM) logical volumes, which operate at the block level, Btrfs subvolumes are based on file extents. Subvolumes appear as directories. You can manipulate them like any other directory, including renaming or moving them.

One of the primary purposes of subvolumes is to be explicitly included or excluded from snapshots. When using a snapshot to roll back the system, we need to ensure that data such as users' home directories, Web and FTP server contents or log files do not get lost or overwritten during a rollback. This is achieved by excluding certain Btrfs subvolumes from snapshots. For more information and the list of excluded subvolumes, see .

section.title: Btrfs Snapshots
section.para: A snapshot in Btrfs is a subvolume that shares data with another subvolume. A new snapshot carries the initial content of the original subvolume. Snapshots use the copy-on-write capabilities of Btrfs, so the system creates them quickly with minimal disk space usage. You can use snapshots to capture the state of a file system at a point in time and to roll back to a previous state if needed.

section.title: Disk space usage of snapshots
section.para: When the system creates a snapshot, the snapshot and the original point to the same blocks in the file system. Initially, a snapshot therefore occupies almost no additional disk space, apart from its metadata. If data in the original file system is modified, Btrfs copies the changed blocks and keeps the old blocks for the snapshot. Therefore, a snapshot occupies the same amount of space as the data modified. Over time, the space that a snapshot allocates grows constantly. As a consequence, deleting files from a Btrfs file system that contains snapshots might not free disk space.

Snapshots always reside on the same partition or subvolume where the snapshot was taken. You cannot store snapshots on a different file system. As a result, partitions that contain snapshots must be larger than partitions without snapshots. The exact amount depends strongly on the number of snapshots you keep and the amount of data modifications. As a guideline, plan for twice as much space as you normally would. &snapper; cleans up old snapshots automatically to prevent disks from running out of space. For more information, see .
